lessons.title: Organic Certification Record Requirements
lessons.body: Organic certification opens premium markets in Africa, from EU exporters to local supermarkets. To get certified, you must prove you follow organic rules for at least 3 years before your first harvest. That means keeping detailed records from day one. Start with a field map showing every plot, and note the last date any prohibited substance was used. For each field, record all inputs: compost, manure, botanical sprays. Write down the source, amount, and date. For example, '10 kg chicken manure from Kuku Farm, applied to Plot A on 15 March 2025.' You also need a seed log: variety, supplier, and whether it is organic or treated. If treated, it cannot be used. Keep a harvest log: date, field, quantity, and how it was stored. Your records must be traceable from seed to sale. Use a simple notebook or a spreadsheet on your phone. Many certifiers like Ecocert or CERES require you to keep records for at least 5 years. They will check your records against your actual practices during an annual inspection. If you sell to a cooperative, they may need copies. Also keep receipts for any purchased organic inputs. A common mistake is mixing organic and conventional produce in storage. Record separate lot numbers and storage locations. Train your workers to write in the log immediately after each activity. A waterproof notebook and a pen tied to a post in the field works well. At the end of each season, review your records with your certifier's checklist. Missing records can delay certification by a year. So start simple, be consistent, and treat your record book as your proof of organic integrity.

lessons.title: Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) Records
lessons.body: Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) certification is required by many buyers, especially for export fruits and vegetables. GAP covers food safety, worker health, and environmental care. To pass a GAP audit, you need records for every step. First, a farm map with all fields, storage, and packing areas. Then, a water test record: test your irrigation water for E. coli at least once a year. Keep the lab report. Next, a fertilizer log: date, field, type, rate, and method. For example, 'NPK 17-17-17, 50 kg per hectare, broadcast on Plot 3, 10 June 2025.' You also need a pesticide log (see Lesson 4). Worker training records: who was trained, when, and on what topic (e.g., safe pesticide handling). A hygiene log for toilets and handwashing stations: check daily and record. Harvest records: date, field, harvest crew, and quantity. Also keep a cleaning log for harvest tools and crates. For post-harvest, record storage temperature and humidity if you have a cold room. Traceability is key: each harvest lot must link back to the field and inputs. Use a simple coding system: farm initials, field number, date. For example, 'KFM-F3-20250610' for Kilimo Farm Field 3 on 10 June 2025. Keep all records for at least 2 years. During an audit, the inspector will pick a lot number and ask you to show all records for that lot. If you cannot, you fail. So store records in one place, like a ring binder with plastic sleeves. Use a checklist from your buyer or from GlobalG.A.P. to self-audit before the real inspection. A well-kept record system is your best tool for passing GAP.

lessons.title: Traceability and Lot Numbers
lessons.body: Traceability means you can follow a product from the field to the customer, and back. It is required by law in many countries and by buyers. The key tool is a lot number. A lot number is a unique code for a batch of produce. For example, 'TOM-20250615-01' means tomatoes harvested on 15 June 2025, first lot of the day. You must assign a lot number at harvest. Write it on the harvest crate, on the delivery note, and in your record book. Then, every time you move or process that lot, record the lot number. If you mix lots, you lose traceability. So keep lots separate. For each lot, record: field name, harvest date, harvest crew, inputs used (fertilizer, pesticide) with dates, and quantity. Also record storage location and any treatments (e.g., washing, waxing). When you sell, record the buyer, date, quantity, and lot number. If a customer complains, you can trace back to the field and see if there was a problem. For example, if a buyer finds pesticide residue, you check your pesticide log for that lot. If you used a banned chemical, you know which field and when. That helps you fix the problem and prevent it. Use a simple numbering system: farm code (2 letters), field number (1-2 digits), date (YYMMDD), and sequence (01, 02). Write it with a permanent marker on crates. For bulk bins, use a tag. Keep a master log of all lot numbers. For small farms, a notebook works. For larger farms, use a spreadsheet or a free app like Farmbrite. Train your workers to never mix lots. During an audit, the inspector will pick a lot number and ask for all records. If you can show them in 5 minutes, you pass. If you search for hours, you fail. So make lot numbers a habit.

lessons.title: Pesticide Application Logs
lessons.body: Pesticide logs are the most important record for food safety. Buyers and auditors will check them first. You must record every pesticide application, even if it is organic. For each application, write: date, time, field, crop, pest, product name, active ingredient, rate (e.g., 500 ml per hectare), amount used, water volume, applicator name, and weather conditions (wind, temperature). Also record the pre-harvest interval (PHI) â the number of days between spraying and harvest. For example, if the label says 7 days, and you spray on 1 June, you cannot harvest before 8 June. Write that in the log. After spraying, record the re-entry interval (REI) â when workers can go back in the field. Use a dedicated notebook or a form. Keep it with the pesticides in a locked store. Never use a banned pesticide. Check with your local agricultural office for a list of approved products. In Kenya, for example, the Pest Control Products Board (PCPB) lists approved pesticides. In Nigeria, use NAQS. For organic certification, only use products allowed by your certifier. Record the name of the person who mixed and applied. Also record the calibration of your sprayer: date, nozzle type, and output. After application, record the disposal of empty containers: triple-rinsed and punctured, then taken to a collection point. Keep all receipts for pesticide purchases. During an audit, the inspector will compare your log with your harvest records. If you sprayed and harvested too soon, you fail. So always double-check the PHI. A simple rule: write it down immediately after spraying, before you forget. Use a waterproof pen. If you make a mistake, cross it out, write the correct entry, and initial. Never erase. A clean, honest log builds trust and keeps your market access.

lessons.title: Animal Health and Treatment Records
lessons.body: If you keep livestock, animal health records are essential for certification and for selling to processors or exporters. You need to record every treatment, vaccination, and health event. Start with individual animal identification: ear tags, brands, or names. For each animal, keep a record card or a page in a logbook. Write: species, breed, sex, date of birth or purchase, and source. For treatments, record: date, animal ID, diagnosis or reason, product name, active ingredient, dose, route (injection, oral, topical), and withdrawal period. The withdrawal period is the time after treatment before you can sell milk, meat, or eggs. For example, if you treat a cow with oxytetracycline, the milk withdrawal might be 3 days and meat withdrawal 28 days. Write those dates clearly. Also record the person who administered the treatment. For vaccinations, record: vaccine name, batch number, expiry date, date given, and next due date. Keep a herd health calendar. For example, in East Africa, you might vaccinate cattle against East Coast Fever (ECF) at 3 months, and against Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD) every 6 months. Record every visit from a vet or animal health assistant: date, name, reason, and advice given. If an animal dies, record the date, cause (if known), and disposal method. For milk, keep a daily milk record: animal ID, litres, and any abnormalities (e.g., mastitis). If you sell milk, you need to show that treated cows are not milked during the withdrawal period. Use a red tag or separate the animal. During an audit, the inspector will pick an animal and ask for its full health record. If you cannot show it, you fail. So keep records in a sturdy folder, one page per animal. Use a simple table. Update it every time you treat. This protects your animals, your customers, and your certification.

lessons.title: Preparing for Audits and Inspections
lessons.body: An audit is a check that your records match your practices. It can be for organic, GAP, or a buyer's own standard. To prepare, start 3 months before. Get the checklist from your certifier or buyer. Go through each item and check if you have the record. For example, if the checklist asks for 'water test report', do you have one from the last 12 months? If not, get it done. Organize your records in one place. Use a ring binder with sections: farm map, input logs, harvest logs, pesticide logs, training records, and receipts. Label each section. For digital records, keep a folder on your phone or computer, and back it up. Make sure your records are up to date. If you missed an entry, write it in now, but mark it as 'late entry' and explain why. Honesty is better than gaps. Do a self-audit: pick a lot number and try to trace it from field to sale. Can you find all records in 10 minutes? If not, improve your filing. Train your workers on what to say. The inspector may ask a worker: 'What do you do after spraying?' The worker should say: 'I record it in the log and respect the PHI.' Practice with them. On audit day, be polite and calm. Have your records ready. The inspector will walk your farm. They will look at storage, toilets, and worker safety. They may take samples. If they find a non-compliance, they will give you time to fix it. Usually, you get 30 days. Write a corrective action plan and send it. After the audit, keep a copy of the report. If you pass, you get a certificate. Display it. If you fail, learn from it and try again. Many certifiers offer a pre-audit for a fee. That is a good investment. Remember, an audit is not a test; it is a way to prove you are doing the right thing. Good records make it easy.

quiz.q: How many years of records do most organic certifiers require before certification?
quiz.explanation: Most organic certifiers require at least 3 years of records to prove organic practices.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical record required for organic certification?
quiz.explanation: Employee salary records are not part of organic certification requirements.

quiz.q: What is the minimum time you should keep organic records?
quiz.explanation: Most certifiers require records to be kept for at least 5 years.

quiz.q: Which of these is a prohibited input in organic farming?
quiz.explanation: Synthetic fertilizers are prohibited in organic farming.

quiz.q: What should you do if you mix organic and conventional produce in storage?
options: B) Record separate lot numbers and storage locations
quiz.explanation: To maintain organic integrity, you must keep them separate and record lot numbers.

quiz.q: How often should you test irrigation water for E. coli under GAP?
quiz.explanation: GAP requires at least annual water testing for E. coli.

quiz.q: What does GAP stand for?
quiz.explanation: GAP stands for Good Agricultural Practices.

quiz.q: Which record is NOT typically required for GAP certification?
quiz.explanation: Vehicle registration is not a standard GAP record.

quiz.q: How long should you keep GAP records?
quiz.explanation: GAP typically requires records to be kept for at least 2 years.

quiz.q: What is a key element of GAP regarding harvest tools?
quiz.explanation: A cleaning log for harvest tools is required to ensure food safety.

quiz.q: What is traceability?
options: B) Following a product from field to customer
quiz.explanation: Traceability is the ability to follow a product through all stages of production and distribution.

quiz.q: What is a lot number?
options: A) A number for a plot of land
B) A unique code for a batch of produce
C) A number for a tractor
D) A number for a worker
quiz.explanation: A lot number identifies a specific batch of produce for traceability.

quiz.q: When should you assign a lot number?
quiz.explanation: Lot numbers are assigned at harvest to link produce to its field and date.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a lot number in an audit?
options: B) To trace records for a specific batch
quiz.explanation: Inspectors use lot numbers to trace all records for a batch of produce.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good practice for lot numbers?
options: A) Use the same number for all lots
B) Write with permanent marker on crates
quiz.explanation: Writing lot numbers clearly on crates helps maintain traceability.

quiz.q: What is the pre-harvest interval (PHI)?
options: A) Time between planting and harvest
B) Time between spraying and harvest
C) Time between harvest and sale
quiz.explanation: PHI is the number of days between pesticide application and harvest.

quiz.q: What should you record in a pesticide log?
quiz.explanation: A complete pesticide log includes product, applicator, weather, and other details.

quiz.q: What is the re-entry interval (REI)?
options: A) Time before you can spray again
B) Time before workers can enter the field
C) Time before you can sell
D) Time before you can eat
quiz.explanation: REI is the time after pesticide application before workers can safely enter the field.

quiz.q: Where should you keep pesticide records?
options: B) With the pesticides in a locked store
quiz.explanation: Keeping records with pesticides ensures they are available and secure.

quiz.q: What should you do with empty pesticide containers?
options: B) Triple-rinse and puncture, then dispose properly
quiz.explanation: Triple-rinsing and puncturing prevents reuse and makes them safe for disposal.

quiz.q: What is the withdrawal period for animal treatments?
options: A) Time before you can treat again
B) Time before you can sell milk or meat
C) Time before you can vaccinate
D) Time before you can breed
quiz.explanation: The withdrawal period is the time after treatment before animal products can be sold.

quiz.q: What should you record for each animal treatment?
quiz.explanation: All these details are essential for animal health records.

quiz.q: How should you identify animals for record keeping?
options: B) By ear tags or brands
quiz.explanation: Ear tags or brands provide unique identification for each animal.

quiz.q: What is a herd health calendar?
options: B) A schedule for vaccinations and treatments
quiz.explanation: A herd health calendar schedules vaccinations and other health events.

quiz.q: What should you do if an animal dies?
options: B) Record date, cause, and disposal method
quiz.explanation: Recording death details is important for traceability and health monitoring.

quiz.q: How long before an audit should you start preparing?
quiz.explanation: Starting 3 months ahead gives time to gather missing records and fix issues.

quiz.q: What is a self-audit?
quiz.explanation: A self-audit is when you check your own records against the checklist before the official audit.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a non-compliance during an audit?
options: B) Write a corrective action plan
quiz.explanation: A corrective action plan shows how you will fix the problem within a given time.

quiz.q: Why is it important to train workers for an audit?
options: A) So they can answer inspector questions correctly
B) So they can hide mistakes
C) So they can take the blame
D) So they can ignore the audit
quiz.explanation: Trained workers can confidently explain practices to the inspector.

quiz.q: What is a pre-audit?
options: A) An audit before the real audit
B) An audit after the real audit
quiz.explanation: A pre-audit is a practice audit to identify and fix issues before the official inspection.
